shower.thought: We spend our whole lives trying to organize chaos, but maybe we're just adding more chaos to the act of organizing.
The saddest part about growing up isn't losing your sense of wonder—it's realizing most people around you lost theirs first.
You'll never know if the way you see red is the same as how anyone else sees it, so the most basic thing you experience might be completely unique to you alone.
We call it "falling" asleep but we're actually "rising" into another consciousness—the language got it backwards.
Your phone knows more about your actual priorities than you do, because it's watching where your attention really goes, not where you think it should go.
Most of us are afraid of ending up alone, but we're already practicing it every time we're lost in our own thoughts around other people.
The reason we fear death might not be about ceasing to exist—it might be that we're terrified of discovering whether anything mattered at all.
You're always the background character in everyone else's story, no matter how important you feel in your own.
Somewhere right now, someone is experiencing their last moment as a person who hasn't lost someone yet, and they don't know it.
The only time you're truly present is when you're bored, because you're not recording the moment for later.
We treat our bodies like rental cars—changing the oil, fixing the dents—but we never really own the thing we're driving.
Your biggest fear is probably something that would seem trivial to you ten years ago, which means it'll probably seem trivial again ten years from now.
Nostalgia is just mourning something that's still alive, which might be worse than actually losing it.
You can spend decades building a reputation in seconds to destroy it, but you can destroy a reputation in seconds and spend decades trying to rebuild it—the math has never been fair.
The moments that change your life the most are usually the ones that felt completely ordinary while they were happening.
We're obsessed with living in the moment, but the present is literally already gone by the time you become aware of it—you're always living in memory.
Your laugh is the only sound your own ears never really hear the way other people do.
If you've ever forgotten someone's name mid-conversation with them, you've experienced a small death—they disappeared from your mind while still standing in front of you.
The people who say they're "bad with names" might just be people who don't expect to see someone twice.
We spend so much time worrying about what we'll regret, but we almost never regret the things we actually do—we only regret the things we didn't do, which we can't even fully imagine.

motivational.thought: The only way to do great work is to love what you do. — Steve Jobs
Your limitation—it's only your lack of vision. — Unknown
Progress is messy. Expect it to be. — Unknown
We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit. — Aristotle
The man who moves a mountain begins by carrying away small stones. — Confucius
You miss 100% of the shots you don't take. — Wayne Gretzky
Fear is the tax on the things worth doing. — Unknown
Everything you want is on the other side of fear. — Jack Canfield
The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is now. — Chinese Proverb
Comparison is the thief of joy. — Theodore Roosevelt
Your problem isn't lack of talent. It's lack of belief. — Unknown
The only person you are destined to become is the person you decide to be. — Ralph Waldo Emerson
Small progress is still progress. — Unknown

Everything worthwhile is uphill. — Unknown
Mastery is the progressive deepening of skill. — George Leonard

darkjoke.thought:
My therapist asked if I ever thought about hurting myself.
I said, "Only when you send me your invoice."

I told my friend I was going to start a support group for people with no friends.
He asked when the first meeting was.

My grandfather said, "Your generation is too reliant on technology."
I said, "You're right," and unplugged his life support.
I'm reading a book on the history of glue—can't put it down.

My wife asked if I was seeing someone else.
I said, "Only when I look in the mirror, and honestly, I'm not impressed with what I see either."

I got fired from my job at the suicide hotline.
Apparently, "you've reached the right place" is not the correct greeting.

My doctor told me I have six months to live.
I said, "I can't pay the bill."
He said, "Then you have a year."

I asked my boss for a raise because I had three kids to support.
He said, "That's not my problem."
I said, "Exactly—they're yours now."

People keep saying I need to be more optimistic.
I told them the cancer probably agrees.

My girlfriend said she needed space.
I said, "No problem," and pushed her out of the car.

I went to a restaurant that only serves food from your childhood.
Turns out it's just an orphanage.

My son asked me what the difference between understanding and empathy is.
I said, "If I hear you bombed your test, I understand."
He said, "And empathy?"
I said, "I'd pretend to be shocked."

I told my therapist I was afraid of commitment.
He said, "Let's talk about it," and immediately booked me for 52 more sessions.

My dad always said, "Money can't buy happiness."
Then he died and left me his inheritance.
I've never been more miserable.

I asked the dentist why he wanted to be a dentist.
He said, "I love helping people."
I said, "That's sweet. So why did you choose this?"

I told my friend his motivational speaking wasn't working.
He said, "Give me one more chance."
Now he's a funeral director—and business is booming.

At my intervention, everyone said I had a drinking problem.
I said, "I don't have a problem—you do."
Then I left to find people who appreciated me.
I'm now drinking alone, which solved everyone's problem.

My kid asked me to explain what a budget is.
I said, "It's the difference between what you need and what you can afford."
He asked, "So we're poor?"
I said, "No, we're just budgeting creatively."

I went to a wellness retreat called "Finding Your Purpose."
Turns out my purpose is wasting money on wellness retreats.

My ex-wife said I was emotionally unavailable.
I didn't respond to that text for three weeks, which I think proved her point.
